name: Champhung, under the source's group statement for 'Tangkhul languages'
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Mortensen, David. 2003. Comparative Tangkhul. Unpublished qualifying paper, University of California, Berkeley, dated 17 December 2003, 73 pp. Self-archived PDF (http://www.davidmortensen.org/papers/comparative_tangkhul.pdf), the Internet Archive Machine copy.
catalog_locator: Sec. 3.1 'Prefixes and Stress', pp. 11-12 (pp. 11-12 of 73; page break after 'one or two unstressed (light syllable)'); also sec. 3 p. 11 item 1, sec. 3.2 p. 12 (examples), sec. 1.1.1 p. 4 (Champhung known only from Brown 1837), sec. 1.2.1 pp. 8-9 (data sources), sec. 1.2.2 p. 9 (stressed allophone of schwa in roots).
catalog_quote: In Tangkhul languages, stress is always predictable. Only roots bear stress, and prefixes never bear stress. The preferred stress pattern, for a word (and foot), is iambic or anapestic. That is to say, a stem usually consists of a stressed (heavy syllable) root and one or two unstressed (light syllable) prefixes. Suffixes that are not a stem in their own right are not stressed, but these often form part of the same stressed syllable as the root. The unstressed nature of these prefixes is probably the source of their relatively predictable vocalism. In almost all cases, the vowel in a prefix is either a mid-central vowel [ə], or a high vowel [i ~ ɨ].
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (the PDF's metadata: 73 pp., dvipdfm, created 17 Dec 2003; title page 'Comparative Tangkhul, David Mortensen, University of California, Berkeley, December 17, 2003'). extracted text shows section '3.1 Prefixes and Stress' starting at the foot of p.11 and continuing on p.12; the quoted passage is there word for word, the page break falling after 'one or two unstressed (light syllable)' / 'prefixes.' The section immediately before (sec. 3, p.11) lists as a synchronic property of prefixes '1. They do not bear stress, unlike root syllables.', and sec. 3.2 (p.12) gives Standard Tangkhul/Kachai examples (kə̀.tà 'far', khə̀.ŋə̀.nà 'hear') with the root as the final, stressed syllable; sec.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is fully predictable from morphology: the (heavy) root syllable is stressed and the one or two (light, schwa- or high-vowel) prefix syllables before it are unstressed, giving an iambic or anapestic stem; suffixes that are not stems are also unstressed. In prefixed words this means stress on the second or third syllable (the root), not the first. Unstressed prefixes take a reduced vowel and a predictable (default) tone, while root syllables carry lexical tone (three tones in Standard Tangkhul).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author says stress 'is always predictable'. Prefix tone may be contrastive in some numerals and nouns (sec. 3.2), but that concerns tone, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level (prefix + root + suffix), citation-form lexical data from field work and dictionaries. The claim is made for 'Tangkhul languages' as a group and rests on the author's own Standard Tangkhul (Ukhrul), Kachai and Huishu data; the same paper states (p.4) that Champhung, the only lect under nort3287, 'is known only from a wordlist provided by Brown (1837)', so no Champhung-specific stress observation exists.
new_statements.identity_note: nort3287 is Glottolog's node for the Champhung village lect (western Ukhrul district, Manipur), attested only by Capt. Gordon's wordlist in Brown 1837; Mortensen 2003 (Fig. 3, p.5) is the source of the 'North-Central' label, with Champhung as its only member. The quoted stress statement is a group-level generalization over 'Tangkhul languages' that Mortensen bases on his own data from Standard Tangkhul/Ukhrul (= East-Central Tangkhul Naga, tang1336, iso nmf), Kachai (East-Central per Mortensen; Glottolog places it under tang1336) and Huishu (= Northern Tangkhul Naga, nort3286). It is first-hand for those lects and only an extrapolation for Champhung, which the same paper says is known solely from a wordlist. The statement should be cross-filed to tang1336 (where our earlier reading listed Mortensen 2003 as unreachable and had only the second-hand StressTyp2 'initial stress' template, which this source contradicts) and to nort3286; symlinks and a note were added under The living village dialect ('Champhung tui', Wikipedia) has no published description found in OpenAlex, Crossref, archive.org or Shodhganga.

sources.note: Sec. 3.1 'Prefixes and Stress' pp.11-12: stress in Tangkhul languages is always predictable; only roots bear stress, prefixes never do; preferred word/foot pattern iambic or anapestic (one or two unstressed light prefix syllables + stressed heavy root); non-stem suffixes unstressed. Group-level claim from the author's Standard Tangkhul (Ukhrul), Kachai and Huishu field data. Sec. 1.1.1 p.4: 'The Champhung language is known only from a wordlist provided by Brown (1837)'; Fig. 3 p.5 places Champhung alone under 'North-Central'.

sources.citation: Brown, Nathan. 1837. Comparison of Indo-Chinese languages. Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal 6(2): 1023-1038.
sources.note: The sole primary attestation of Champhung: Capt. Gordon's 12-language wordlist (Champhung column pp.1034-1035). Gordon's covering letter (pp.1028-1029) discusses only mutual intelligibility among Tangkhul villages; Brown's general remarks on 'intonations' (p.1027) concern Tai, Chinese and Burmese. Nothing on Champhung stress or accent.
